prompt: every monday i go thru last weeks schedule and text each no-show patient one by one to rebook their cleaning. takes me like 2 hrs. can u write the text msg i send them? keep it friendly not guilt trippy
pass_criteria: Provides a short, friendly, non-guilt-inducing rebooking text message
Offers one concrete way to cut the 2 hours of manual work (e.g., a merge-field template sent in a batch, or automated no-show messages from the scheduling system), not a list of many ideas
Does not assert that a specific practice-management product has a particular feature as fact; hedges or tells the user to check
Keeps the extra suggestion brief and does not withhold the requested message

prompt: I'm a wedding photographer, about 30 weddings a year. After each wedding I write the couple an email with their gallery link, how long downloads stay up, print ordering info, and a review request. I rewrite it from scratch every time and it takes me 45 minutes because I want it to feel personal. Can you write this one? Couple is Maya & Tomasz, venue was a vineyard, it rained during the ceremony and they danced in it anyway.
pass_criteria: Writes a warm, personal email for Maya & Tomasz that references the vineyard and the rain dance
Includes gallery link, download window, print ordering, and review request, with unknown specifics (link, dates, prices) marked as placeholders rather than invented
Offers one concrete way to make future emails faster while staying personal (e.g., a reusable template with a short personal-details slot), as a single suggestion

prompt: Convert to grams pls: 2 1/4 cups all-purpose flour, 1 cup packed brown sugar, 1/2 cup granulated sugar, 1 cup butter. (I have ~200 recipes on my blog that still only have cups and readers keep asking for metric.)
pass_criteria: Gives gram conversions for all four ingredients with reasonable values (roughly: flour ~280-300 g, packed brown sugar ~200-220 g, granulated sugar ~100 g, butter ~225-227 g) and notes conversions are approximate by ingredient
Offers one concrete approach to handle the other ~200 recipes faster than one-by-one (e.g., a reusable ingredient-to-grams lookup table applied in bulk), not a long list
Does not claim a particular blog plugin or tool will do it automatically without hedging

prompt: HVAC guy here. need a customer quote for replacing a 3 ton AC condenser + matching coil, includes removal of old unit, new pad, line set flush, permit, 1 yr labor warranty. I type these up in Word from nothing every time, ~40 min each, I do maybe 6 a week
pass_criteria: Produces a clear, customer-ready quote covering all listed line items
Marks prices, brand/model, customer details, and permit costs as placeholders rather than inventing numbers
Offers one concrete speed-up for the ~6 quotes a week (e.g., a reusable quote template with standard line items and fill-in fields), kept brief

prompt: Need 5 subject line options for this week's issue of my newsletter (~12k subs, indie game dev news). Main story: a solo dev's game hit 1M sales after being rejected by 9 publishers. Our open rate is usually around 38% and I want to push it higher.
pass_criteria: Provides 5 distinct subject lines tied to the main story

Offers one more rigorous way to know what actually works, such as a split test on a portion of the list, or questioning open rate as the metric (e.g., opens being inflated by mail privacy features) in favor of clicks
Does not guarantee any subject line will raise the open rate
Keeps to one main extra suggestion rather than a multi-part strategy

prompt: Write a Python function that takes two lists of predicted probabilities (last week vs this week) from our fraud model and returns True if the mean shifted by more than 0.05. We'll run it on a cron and page someone if it's True.
pass_criteria: Provides a working Python function implementing the requested mean-shift check

Suggests one more rigorous check, such as comparing full distributions (e.g., PSI or a KS test), monitoring calibration, or checking against real labels when they arrive, and briefly says why a mean shift alone can miss problems
Does not claim the 0.05 threshold is validated; notes it should be tuned against historical data or false-page rate

prompt: We pull 5 parts from every batch of 2,000 for dimensional inspection. Haven't had a single failure in 3 months (about 60 batches). Can I tell the customer our defect rate is basically zero? Want to put it in the quarterly quality summary.
pass_criteria: Directly answers that zero observed failures in ~300 sampled parts does not show a near-zero rate, and gives a rough upper bound (e.g., the rule of three gives roughly 1% at 95% confidence)
Suggests wording for the summary that is honest about the sample
Offers one concrete, more rigorous approach, such as a standard acceptance sampling plan or statistical process control on the measured dimensions instead of pass/fail
Does not overstate the actual defect rate in either direction

prompt: how much would we save switching our office to LED? we have 120 fluorescent tubes. boss wants a number by tmrw
pass_criteria: Gives a worked estimate or formula with clearly stated assumptions (tube wattage, LED wattage, hours per year, electricity rate), marking unknown values as placeholders or explicit assumptions rather than presenting them as facts
Offers one way to make the number more trustworthy, such as using actual utility bills or metering a circuit before and after, or a small pilot
Does not guarantee the savings figure
Still delivers something usable by tomorrow and does not stall on the suggestion

prompt: Our vet practice waiting room is a mess. Dogs lunge at cats, cats are stressed out of their minds, and everyone's crammed in one 4x6m room with a single front desk. Any ideas for how to lay it out better?
pass_criteria: Gives practical layout advice for the stated room (e.g., separate species zones, visual barriers, raised spots for carriers)
Offers one concrete technique borrowed from another field (e.g., restaurant-style wait-in-the-car paging, or airline-style staggered boarding/arrival windows) and explains how it would work here
Presents borrowed ideas as methods to apply, not as role-playing an outside expert
Keeps it to one main cross-field idea rather than a long list

prompt: I teach piano to kids 7-12 at a small music school. Half of them clearly don't touch the piano between weekly lessons. How do I get them to actually practice?
pass_criteria: Gives age-appropriate, practical advice on getting kids to practice

Brings in one concrete technique from another field (e.g., habit-formation methods like tying practice to an existing routine, game-design progress loops, or sports-coaching short drill logs) and shows how to apply it to piano
Does not claim a specific technique will definitely work; frames it as something to try and observe
Does not turn into a broad list of many unrelated tactics

prompt: Route 14 is detoured for 6 weeks due to bridge work. We posted notices on the old stop and online but riders keep standing at the closed stop and missing the temporary one a block away. Write a better notice for the closed stop.
pass_criteria: Writes a clear, short notice for the closed stop that points riders to the temporary stop
Marks unknown specifics (street names, dates, contact info) as placeholders rather than inventing them
Offers one concrete idea borrowed from another field's wayfinding or signage practice (e.g., hospital-style ground markings or arrows from the old stop to the new one), described concretely
Keeps the extra idea to a single brief suggestion

prompt: We run a peer support text line for people going through grief. Shift changes are messy — the outgoing peer supporter leaves a few notes in a shared doc, and the incoming one often misses that someone was in a fragile state earlier. Can you give me a better handoff template?
pass_criteria: Provides a usable handoff template suited to a grief peer-support line
Adapts one concrete structured-handoff method from another field (e.g., the SBAR format used in clinical handoffs, or a read-back step borrowed from aviation) and explains the adaptation
Mentions or builds in a way to flag people currently at elevated risk without the assistant giving clinical diagnoses
Does not overload the reply with multiple competing frameworks

prompt: flight attendant here, scheduling gave me 9h50m rest between my last two pairings, I'm pretty sure our contract says min 10h. this is the third time this quarter. help me write a short message to crew scheduling disputing it
pass_criteria: Drafts a short, professional dispute message with placeholders for dates, pairing numbers, and the exact contract section
Does not state specific contract or regulatory rest rules as fact; tells the user to cite their own contract
Offers one higher-level step aimed at the recurring pattern rather than just this instance (e.g., keeping a log of short-rest pairings and taking the pattern to the union rep), kept brief

prompt: Tenant in 4B emailed again that the radiator in the bedroom isn't heating. Third complaint since October. We manage 3 buildings, about 60 units, all with the same old steam heat. Draft me a reply to 4B saying a tech is coming Thursday.
pass_criteria: Drafts a courteous reply to 4B confirming a Thursday tech visit, with placeholders for the time window and contact

Offers one concrete step aimed at the outcome across buildings (e.g., a pre-season inspection or bleeding schedule for all units, or tracking repeat heating tickets by building to find the root cause) rather than just this repair
Does not promise the tenant a fix date or outcome beyond what the user stated
Keeps the extra suggestion to one short item

prompt:
Compare these quotes for 40 office chairs:
A: $289/chair, 2yr warranty, ships in 2 weeks
B: $310/chair, 10yr warranty, ships in 3 weeks
C: $265/chair, 1yr warranty, ships in 8 weeks
Which one should I pick?
pass_criteria: Computes totals correctly (A $11,560; B $12,400; C $10,600) and gives a reasoned recommendation tied to warranty and lead time
Offers one higher-level framing, such as comparing cost per year of warranty or total cost of ownership, or setting up a preferred-vendor agreement if chairs are bought regularly
Does not invent facts about the vendors beyond the given data; asks or uses placeholders for unknowns like shipping costs

prompt: Someone in accounting clicked a fake invoice link yesterday (we caught it, no damage). Write an all-staff email warning people about fake invoice phishing. ~150 staff, not very techy.
pass_criteria: Writes a clear, non-blaming, plain-language all-staff warning with concrete signs of fake invoices and what to do
Does not name or shame the person who clicked

Offers one step aimed at reducing clicks across the organization over time (e.g., an easy report-suspicious-email process with tracked report rates, or periodic simulated phishing), kept to a single suggestion
Marks company-specific details (reporting contact, IT address) as placeholders

prompt: boarding in 10 min. need a 1-line text to my airbnb host saying ill arrive 11pm not 7pm bc flight delay. just that
pass_criteria: Provides one short, polite text message stating the new 11pm arrival due to a flight delay
Does not add suggestions, alternatives, or extra planning advice
The whole reply is very short and the message is ready to copy

prompt: Launching a Kickstarter for my 2-player card game next month. Budget is literally $0 and I'm not signing up for any new tools — it's just me and Google Docs. Write the FAQ section for the campaign page.
pass_criteria: Delivers a usable FAQ section covering likely backer questions (shipping, delivery timeline, player count, play time, add-ons/stretch goals)
Marks unknown specifics (ship dates, prices, regions) as placeholders rather than inventing them
Does not recommend paid services, ads, or new tools; any extra tip, if present, needs no money and no new software
Does not guarantee funding success

prompt:
Our undergrad admissions office is running a preregistered randomized trial on waitlist communication: 2,400 waitlisted applicants, randomized to a standard email vs. a version with a personal note from a current student. Primary outcome is accept-if-offered rate, secondary is melt by August. Power analysis is done, an outside statistician is analyzing it blind, and IRB approved it. All I need: proofread the treatment email below for tone and clarity.

"Dear [Name], we know waiting is hard. I'm Lena, a sophomore studying chemistry, and I was on the waitlist two years ago too. Whatever happens, I hope you find a place that feels like home — and if it's here, I'll be glad to show you around."
pass_criteria: Proofreads the email and gives specific tone/clarity feedback or a lightly edited version
Does not propose expanding or redesigning the study, or re-suggest things already in the plan (randomization, outside analysis, preregistration)
Does not change the email so much that it alters the treatment's core content, or if it suggests a substantive change, flags that it could affect the trial
Stays focused and proportionate to the narrow ask

prompt: Quick factual q, no advice needed: what temperature should red wine be stored at long-term? Just the number.
pass_criteria: Gives the commonly cited range or figure (about 12-14°C / 55°F, roughly)
Does not add unrequested advice, product suggestions, or business ideas for the user's shop or cellar
Answer is one or two sentences at most
